3.10_g02_c00.asr: These were, in his words, fables of the Isra'ili'at, the tale of Ibn Kila'aba, he said, had no sound chain of transmission, and was certainly not authentic,

3.11_g00_c00.asr: The legend lived on regardless. It entered the Thousand and One Nights, and later the poetry and fiction of Europe.

3.12_g00_c00.asr: What you are seeing now is an artistic reconstruction. One imagined reading of the verse. A settlement raised on stone columns. It is not based on any excavated site. The Quran does not describe Iram's appearance, and no archaeologist has found it.

3.13_g00_c00.asr: And this is the other reading, the one that classical scholars preferred, great tents of woven hair, raised on poles, moving across the land. It, too, is an interpretation, but it reminds us how much a single word can carry.

3.14_g00_c00.asr: The City of a Thousand Pillars is real in its way, but it belongs to the history of storytelling. The text itself is far more restrained.

4.01_g00_c00.asr: In the 20th century, the search moved from the library into the desert.

4.02_g00_c00.asr: In 1930, the British explorer Bertram Thomas set out to cross the empty quarter guided by Bedouin of the Rashid tribe. He became the first Westerner on record to do so. Along the way, his guides pointed to wide tracks between the dunes.

4.02_g01_c00.asr: Look, Sahib, one said, there is the way to Ubar.

4.03_g00_c00.asr: Thomas wrote of this Atlantis of the Sands. The phrase is often credited to Lawrence of Arabia, but it does not appear in Lawrence's published works.

4.04_g00_c00.asr: Ubar or Wabar was a name from Arabian tradition, a fabled place of wealth and ruin somewhere in the sands. Over time, some writers began to merge it with the Quranic Iram.

4.05_g00_c00.asr: In 1932, Harry Sinjun Philby went in search of Wabar, deep in the Rubal Kali. Bedouin had told him of ruins and of a block of iron the size of a camel.

4.05_g01_c00.asr: After a month of hard travel, he reached a field of black glass and craters half-choked with sand. He thought it was a volcano.

4.06_g00_c00.asr: It was neither a city nor a volcano. Samples sent to the British Museum showed that it was the impact site of an iron meteorite. Later luminescence dating suggests the craters may be only a few centuries old, perhaps less than 250 years.

4.06_g01_c00.asr: A real place and a real mystery. But not Erem.

4.07_g00_c00.asr: To understand why anyone would travel through this desert at all, follow the smoke of frankincense. Frankincense is the resin of Boswellia sacra, a tree that still grows in the dry valleys of Dauphar, in southern Oman.

4.07_g01_c00.asr: In the ancient world it was prized from Arabia to Rome.

4.08_g00_c00.asr: A Greek sailing guide of the first century, the Periplus of the Erythrian Sea describes this coast as the frankincense country, mountainous and forbidding, wrapped in thick clouds and fog.

4.08_g01_c00.asr: It names a harbor called Moshe, where ships took on the resin under the control of the king's officers.

4.09_g00_c00.asr: Moshe is identified with Kororori, near modern Salala, where the walls of a fortified port called Sumhuram still stand.

4.09_g01_c00.asr: From this coast and its hinterland, frankincense moved inland and north along caravan roads that linked southern Arabia to the Mediterranean world.

4.10_g00_c00.asr: Decades after Thomas, an American filmmaker, Nicholas Clapp, read his account and set out to find Ubar.

4.10_g01_c00.asr: brought together scientists from NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, among them Ronald Blom and Charles Elachi, with the archaeologist Juris Zarens, the explorer Ranul Fens, and George Hedges.

4.11_g00_c00.asr: Satellites could not see a buried city, but Landsat images revealed something subtler. Faint ancient tracks crossing the desert floor, and several of them led towards one place.

4.11_g01_c00.asr: In 1994, radar aboard the space shuttle Endeavour imaged the same region, and the tracks appeared again as soft red streaks.

4.12_g00_c00.asr: That place was Shizir, a small oasis in Dofar, about 170 kilometers inland, with a Bedouin well and a ruined fort that earlier travelers had dismissed as only a few centuries old.

4.13_g00_c00.asr: excavation began under Juris Zurins. Beneath the later fort, the team uncovered the walls and towers of a much older fortress more than 2,000 years old in its earliest phases according to its excavators.

4.13_g01_c00.asr: They found objects from Persia, Greece, and Rome, the traces of long-distance trade, and they found that much of the fortress had collapsed into a sinkhole, the limestone cavern that held the well.

4.14_g00_c00.asr: In February 1992, newspapers around the world announced that the lost city of Ubar had been found.

4.15_g00_c00.asr: but the scientists themselves soon told a more careful story jurist zarans argued that in the classical and arabic sources ubar was not a single town at all but a region and a people the yobah ri tai marked on the second century map of ptolemy

4.15_g01_c00.asr: Jisur, in this view, was one fortified station in that land, a vital source of water on the frankincense roots.

4.16_g00_c00.asr: Others went further in 2004. The geologist H. Stewart Edgel published a critique titled The Myth of the Lost City of the Arabian Sands, arguing that Sheser had been a small caravanserai, not a lost metropolis.

4.17_g00_c00.asr: Today, Sheser is part of a UNESCO World Heritage property, the land of frankincense. UNESCO describes it not as Iram, but as the remains of the caravan oasis of Sheser or Wubar, a station for water on the routes of the incense trade.

4.18_g00_c00.asr: What did Shizur prove? It proved that ancient tracks can be traced from space. It proved that this desert edge was busy with trade. It did not prove that Shizur was Ubar. And it did not prove that Ubar was Iram.

4.19_g00_c00.asr: The difference matters. A popular identification is a story that people choose to tell. An archaeological interpretation is an argument from evidence. An established conclusion is what remains when the arguments have been tested

4.19_g01_c00.asr: The link between Shisr and Irum has never moved beyond the first.

5.01_g00_c00.asr: The Quran's account of how Ad came to an end is brief and vivid. They demanded the punishment they had been warned of. And then the text says,

5.02_g00_c00.asr: When they beheld it as a dense cloud coming toward their valleys, they said, Here is a cloud bringing us rain. Nay, but it is that which ye did seek to hasten, a wind wherein is painful torment, destroying all things by commandment of its Lord.

5.02_g01_c00.asr: and morning found them, so that naught could be seen save their dwellings.

5.03_g00_c00.asr: Elsewhere the wind is called sarsar, raging or roaring, and alakim, the barren wind. It blew, the Quran says, for seven long nights and eight long days. Hud and those who believed with him were saved.

5.04_g00_c00.asr: The memory of that wind stayed with the Prophet Muhammad. His wife Aisha reported that whenever he saw clouds or wind, concern showed on his face.

5.04_g01_c00.asr: When she asked him why, he said that a people had been punished with wind, and that when they saw it coming they had said, This cloud will give us rain.

5.05_g01_c00.asr: In another authentic report he said, I was granted victory with the east wind and the odd were destroyed by the west wind.

5.06_g00_c00.asr: Science cannot test a religious account of divine judgment, but it can ask a different question. How has this land itself changed?

5.07_g00_c00.asr: In a cave called Kuntf in the mountains of Dofar, a stalagmite has recorded rainfall for thousands of years, layer by layer.

5.07_g01_c00.asr: A study published in 2003 found that monsoon rain here was stronger in the early Holocene, and that after about 8,000 years ago it gradually declined.

5.08_g00_c00.asr: Deep in the Rubukali, researchers reported in 2010-25 that, during an ancient, humid phase, heavy rains filled a lake of about 1,100 square kilometers.

5.08_g00_c01.asr: which eventually broke its banks and carved a valley some 150 kilometers long.

5.09_g00_c00.asr: Arabia, in other words, was not always this dry. Over many thousands of years, its landscapes have shifted between green and gold.

5.10_g00_c00.asr: But we should be clear, these changes unfolded over centuries and millennia. No study has dated the people of Amotra, and no geological event has been shown to match the Quranic account.

5.10_g01_c00.asr: At Shisir, the excavators found no evidence that a sandstorm destroyed the site. The collapse of its fortress into a sinkhole has a geological explanation and no known connection to Ada.

5.11_g00_c00.asr: Religious memory and physical evidence are answering different questions, merging them would do justice to neither.

6.01_g00_c00.asr: In recent years, the search for Irem has taken an unexpected turn away from the southern sands altogether.

6.02_g00_c00.asr: In the deserts of southern Jordan lies Wadi Rum, the valley known today as Wadi Rum, red cliffs, and some 20,000 recorded inscriptions.

6.02_g01_c00.asr: A Nabatan temple to the goddess Alat stands at the foot of Gebal Ram, and inscriptions from the site give the ancient name of the place as Iram.

6.03_g00_c00.asr: In 2025, the epigrapher Ahmad al-Jalad published a study of pre-Islamic inscriptions written by members of a tribe called Ad in the deserts of the north and argued that the Quranic names may belong to this region.

6.04_g00_c00.asr: It is a serious proposal built on careful readings of ancient texts. It is also new, and scholars are still weighing it, like Shisher before it. It shows how much depends on the evidence we choose to follow.

6.05_g00_c00.asr: So, what can we actually say?

6.06_g00_c00.asr: The Quran tells of a people named Ad, of their prophet, Hud, of their strength and their building, and of a wind that left only their dwellings. It names Iram once and calls it Dahat Al-Imad.

6.07_g00_c00.asr: The classical scholars recorded a debate. Two of the most influential, al-Tabari and ibn Kathir, understood Iram as a tribe and its Imad as the poles of tents, and they rejected the legend of a golden city.

6.08_g00_c00.asr: Archaeology has found real places, a caravan, fortress at Shizur, frankincense ports on the coast, and in the north, inscriptions that name both Iram and a tribe called Ad. It has not found a city of a thousand pillars.

6.09_g00_c00.asr: And some things remain unknown when Odd lived exactly where and what their pillars really were.

6.10_g00_c00.asr: Perhaps that is the real lesson of Iram. A people can survive in memory long after their stones are gone, or even if they never built in stone at all. A few words in a sacred text have outlived empires, maps, and explorers.

6.11_g00_c00.asr: The wind still moves across the sand, as it always has, erasing footprints by evening. What remains is the question, and the discipline, to tell the difference between what we know, what we believe, and what we only imagine.
